results.summary: This analog design combines a simple opamp powered at 3.3V with a DRAM cell and an 8-bit R2R DAC. The opamp inputs are shared with the DRAM bit lines, and digital control pins select write and read operations. The 3.3V output is achieved with level shifting drivers, and the design is intended to be tested by measuring the output voltage on analog pin 0 with a multimeter. The documentation is brief and does not explain the DRAM cell operation or the exact role of the bias control pins.

The EnDecoder encrypts or decrypts a 4-bit code using a 4-bit key, with the mode selected by an input pin. A done output pulses when the operation completes, and the result appears on a 4-bit output. Testing involves feeding a code and key in encrypt mode, then feeding the result back in decrypt mode to recover the original code. No external hardware is required, but the documentation does not specify the encryption algorithm.

TinyTapeStation is a retro gaming console that plays a single pre-loaded game called Gnome Knight, controlled with an NES or SNES gamepad. It outputs 640x480 VGA video and analog audio, and supports standard retro controller layouts with simple remapping. The design requires a gamepad PMOD or direct NES controller wiring, a VGA monitor, and speakers or an amplifier. A silicon test report notes that the game starts up and characters move, though the tester did not have a SNES controller.

This project implements the Blake2s hashing algorithm in Verilog with C firmware support, including secret key support and block streaming. It exposes an 8-bit data input, command and valid handshake signals, and an 8-bit hash output with a valid flag. The documentation is essentially absent beyond the pin names and one-line description, so the exact usage and testing procedure are unclear. The design is notable for being a hardware implementation of a modern cryptographic hash.

The Electronic Voting Machine counts votes for three candidates, with each candidate having a dedicated input button. When the vote_over signal is asserted, voting stops and the results for all three candidates are output as 6-bit binary values. A reset signal clears all counts for a new session. The design is tested with a testbench that simulates button presses and dumps waveforms, but no external hardware is specified.

This is a simple SPI slave controller for reading and writing internal registers. It uses standard SPI signals (NCS, CLK, MOSI, MISO) and also provides a FIFO output serial line. The system clock must be at least four times faster than the SPI clock. Testing requires an external SPI controller connected to the SPI pins, and the documentation includes timing diagrams for read and write transactions.

This is a femtoRV RISC-V implementation that uses external SPI flash and SPI RAM for program and data storage. It provides UART communication for debug messages and an LED output. To use it, an external flash memory must be programmed with the desired application, and a USB-serial dongle is needed for communication. The design is notable for being a compact RISC-V core on a tiny tapeout tile.

This is an 8-bit VHDL implementation of the XORShift random number generator, based on Tzarc's algorithm. It uses the previous output and a counter of generated numbers to produce a new 8-bit output. Testing involves comparing the output with a known-good software implementation by manually clocking the circuit. The design is a straightforward PRNG with no external hardware requirements.

This is a small custom 4-bit CPU with 16 instructions and 16x4-bit storage. It includes a UART receive pin, four input pins, four output pins, and instruction register outputs, along with state signals for program, fetch, decode, and execute phases. The documentation is extremely thin, consisting only of placeholder text like 'TESTETSet' and 'TESTSEt', so the operation and testing procedure cannot be determined. External hardware is mentioned but not specified.

This is a 5-tap FIR filter implemented in VHDL that computes a filtered output from the last five input samples. Filter coefficients can be loaded serially over five clock cycles and updated with a load signal. The design requires no external hardware and is tested by feeding coefficients and then applying input samples while observing the filtered output. The documentation provides a clear explanation of the filter operation and testing method.
